10  Running the analysis, and chapter reference

title: Running the analysis, and chapter reference
text:
Key terms
Every term links to the section that defines it, and the three groups follow the three parts of the chapter, so this doubles as a revision map.

Part 1, the shape of a distribution


Distribution

the values a variable takes, and how often

Shape

the outline a histogram makes: peaks, symmetry, tails

Unimodal

having one peak

Symmetric

two halves that mirror each other

Ceiling effect

cases piled up at the top of a scale

Skewness

how far a distribution leans to one side

Standard error

how much a statistic varies from sample to sample

Kurtosis

how heavy the tails are, compared with normal

Leptokurtic

heavier tails than normal

Platykurtic

lighter tails and a flatter peak than normal





Part 2, the normal curve and z-scores


Normal distribution

a symmetric bell-shaped model fixed by its mean and standard deviation

Empirical rule

68, 95 and 99.7 per cent within 1, 2 and 3 SD

Chebyshev’s rule

at least \(1 - 1/k^2\) within \(k\) SD, for any shape

z-score

distance from the mean in standard deviations

Standardising

converting a column to z-scores

Unusual value

a z-score from 2 up to 3, either sign

Extreme value

a z-score of 3 or more, either sign





Part 3, areas, percentiles and normality


Standard normal distribution

the normal distribution with mean 0 and SD 1

Area under the curve

the share of cases between two values

Percentile from the normal model

\(\bar{x} + z s\) for the z that cuts off the share

Q-Q plot

sorted data against normal predictions

Shapiro-Wilk test

a test of how closely data follow a normal pattern

APA style

the standard form for reporting statistics in a written report

p-value

below 0.05, a departure larger than chance

title: Running the analysis, and chapter reference
text:
Formula review



Table 2.19: Every formula used in this chapter









Quantity
Formula




z-score, sample
\(z = \dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\)


z-score, population
\(z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\)


Value from a z-score
\(x = \bar{x} + z \times s\)


Skewness, as JASP reports it
\(\dfrac{n}{(n-1)(n-2)} \sum \left(\dfrac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\right)^3\)


Skewness ratio
\(\dfrac{\text{skewness}}{\text{SE of skewness}}\), beyond \(\pm 2\) flags skew


Kurtosis ratio
\(\dfrac{\text{excess kurtosis}}{\text{SE of kurtosis}}\), beyond \(\pm 2\) flags unusual tails


Empirical rule
about 68%, 95%, 99.7% within \(1, 2, 3\) SD


Chebyshev’s rule
at least \(1 - \dfrac{1}{k^2}\) within \(k\) SD, for \(k > 1\)


Share above \(z\)
\(1 -\) area below \(z\)


Share below \(-z\)
area above \(+z\)


Share between \(z_1\) and \(z_2\)
area below \(z_2 -\) area below \(z_1\)


Normal notation
\(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma)\), and \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\)

Activity 3: Standardised scores (40 minutes)

Step 10. Create the z-scores

JASPPocketStat


Click the + at the right-hand end of the column headers to add a computed column. Name it Wait_z, choose the R formula box, and enter:
(Waiting_Time_Mins - mean(Waiting_Time_Mins)) / sd(Waiting_Time_Mins)
The formula is the z-score from part 2, \(z = (x - \bar{x}) / s\), written for the whole column at once:

Waiting_Time_Mins is \(x\), each customer’s own wait
mean(Waiting_Time_Mins) is \(\bar{x}\), 45.455 minutes
sd(Waiting_Time_Mins) is \(s\), 11.905 minutes. R’s sd() divides by \(n - 1\), so it gives the same sample standard deviation JASP reported in step 6.

JASP works through the column one row at a time. Respondent 1 waited 28 minutes and gets \((28 - 45.455) \div 11.905 = -1.466\), the value you calculated by hand in worked example 2.5. Check that row 1 of Wait_z reads -1.466 before you go on.
Leave its type as Scale. A z-score is a measurement with equal gaps, so scale is correct.



Creating the z-score column




Tap Analyse and choose Z-scores & empirical rule, then pick Waiting_Time_Mins and run it. PocketStat applies the z-score formula from part 2, \(z = (x - \bar{x}) / s\), to every row, using the column’s mean of 45.455 and standard deviation of 11.905.
It reports a summary of the z-scores, set out in the next three steps, and shows no z-score for each row. To find one customer’s z-score, apply the formula yourself, the way worked example 2.5 does.



Z-scores & empirical rule with Waiting_Time_Mins chosen







Step 11. Check the standardising worked

JASPPocketStat


Run Descriptive Statistics on Wait_z with mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum ticked. The standard deviation should be 1.000, the minimum -2.810 and the maximum 3.742.
The mean should be zero. JASP may print it as a tiny number in scientific notation, such as \(2.588 \times 10^{-16}\). Moving the decimal point 16 places gives 0.0000000000000002588, which is zero apart from the computer’s rounding. A standardised column always has a mean of zero.



Descriptives for the z-score column




On Results, read the first rows: n is 200, the mean 45.455 and the standard deviation 11.905. These are the two numbers used to build every z-score in the column.



The mean and standard deviation used for the z-scores







Step 12. Compare the data with the empirical rule

JASPPocketStat


Add a second computed column named Wait_z_band, using the R formula box:
cut(abs(Wait_z), breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 10), right = FALSE)
Set its type to Ordinal, then run Descriptive Statistics on it with Frequency tables ticked. The cumulative percent column gives the share within one, two and three standard deviations: 66.5, 96.5 and 99.5.



The z-score bands as a frequency table




Read the three percentage rows. Within one standard deviation: 66.5. Within two: 96.5. Within three: 99.5. PocketStat prints the empirical rule’s 68, 95 and 99.7 beside each for comparison.



The empirical rule check in PocketStat







Step 13. Find the unusual and extreme cases

JASPPocketStat


Run Descriptive Statistics on Wait_z. Under Customizable plots, tick Boxplots and Label outliers, as in step 9.
The vertical axis is now in z-scores, so each point’s distance from the mean reads straight off it. Four points sit beyond the whiskers, each labelled with its row number:

Row 85, above 3, is the extreme case: a wait of 90 minutes at \(z = 3.74\).
Row 58, between 2 and 3 above the mean, is unusual: 77 minutes at \(z = 2.65\).
Rows 149 and 189, between 2 and 3 below the mean, are unusual: 12 and 14 minutes.

The boxplot flags cases beyond its fences, the \(1.5 \times IQR\) rule from chapter 1, so it marks 4 of the 7 cases that step 12 counted at 2 or more standard deviations. The other three, waits of 19, 20 and 21 minutes, sit just inside the lower whisker. Table 2.11 in the chapter lists all seven, with a column showing which ones the fences catch.



A boxplot of the z-scores with the cases beyond the whiskers labelled by row




Read the row observations with |z| > 2, which should be 7, and the note beneath the table, which names the row with the largest z-score: row 85, a wait of 90 minutes, \(z = 3.74\).
The boxplot beside the histogram shows four points beyond the whiskers, two long waits and two short ones, the same four JASP marks. PocketStat leaves the points unlabelled, so match them with Table 2.11 in the chapter, which lists all seven cases with their z-scores.



The count of cases beyond two standard deviations, and the boxplot





Then answer three questions from your own output:

How many of the 200 waits are typical, how many unusual and how many extreme? How does that compare with what a normal curve predicts?
Respondent 85 gave a satisfaction score of 4.50. What would you check before reporting this wait to the manager?

Key takeaways

Look at the shape before you choose a summary or a model.
Judge skewness and kurtosis by their size and by their ratio to the standard error.
The empirical rule applies to distributions close to normal. Chebyshev’s rule applies to any shape.
A z-score places a value in standard deviations from the mean, and it compares values measured in different units.
A value beyond 2 is unusual and beyond 3 is extreme. Both call for a second look at the record.

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Decisions under uncertainty
A decision under uncertainty is a choice made before you know how it will turn out. Booking a venue for 120 people is a decision under uncertainty, because some of the 120 will stay at home. Choosing a vendor is one, because a vendor can deliver late. Promising a date for an event is one, because tasks overrun.
Uncertainty requires structured reasoning. Records of past events show how often people fail to turn up. Past contracts show how often each vendor delivered on time. Previous task managers can estimate typical durations and worst-case delays. A manager who quantifies this evidence can compare options objectively and justify the choice to stakeholders.
Every decision tool in this chapter follows the same eight steps.



Table 3.1: The eight steps of a decision under uncertainty










Step
What you do
Example from the events team




1. State the question
Write the decision as one question
Which vendor should supply the event?


2. List the options
Name every choice under your control
Local vendor or international vendor


3. Name the uncertain events
Name what you cannot control
The vendor delivers on time or late


4. Assign probabilities
Give each event a number from evidence
On time 0.740 for the local vendor


5. Attach the outcomes
Give each path a payoff, a cost or a time
6,943.62 USD if on time


6. Calculate
Combine probabilities and outcomes
The expected value of each option


7. Review the risk
Look at the worst case and its chance
A loss of 1,818.47 USD, with probability 0.260


8. Recommend
Write the choice and the reason
Book the vendor with the higher expected value, if the worst case is affordable






Steps 1 to 3 need judgement and no arithmetic. Steps 4 to 6 are the arithmetic this chapter teaches. Steps 7 and 8 return to judgement, and they decide whether the arithmetic is used well.

Five terms for this chapter
Five terms appear throughout the chapter, and each gets a full section later. You need to recognise all five now, as the following pages use them before their defining sections appear.
A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that states how likely an event is. A probability of 0.83 means the event happens in about 83 cases out of 100.
An event is an outcome you can count in the records: a registered person attended, a vendor delivered late, a task finished on day 16.
An expected value is the average outcome of an uncertain option, with each possible outcome weighted by its probability. Part 2 shows how to calculate one.
A decision tree is a diagram that sets out the options, the uncertain events that follow each option and the outcome at the end of every path.
The critical path is the longest chain of linked tasks in a project. It sets the earliest finishing date, and any delay to a task on it delays the whole project. Part 3 shows how to find it.

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Probability from records
A probability from records is the share of past cases in which an event happened. You count the cases where the event happened and divide by the number of cases the question is about.
\[P(A) = \frac{\text{number of cases in which } A \text{ happened}}{\text{number of cases the question is about}}\]
\(P(A)\) is read as “the probability of \(A\)”. Three properties follow from the definition:

Every probability lies between 0 and 1. A probability of 0 means the event never happened in the records, and 1 means it happened every time.
The probabilities of all the possible outcomes of one variable add to 1. A registered person either attended or did not, so the two probabilities cover every case.
A probability multiplied by 100 is a percentage. A probability of 0.83 and a share of 83 per cent state the same fact.

The probability file holds 100 registration records from past events, one row per person who registered. Each row records whether the person attended, the type of ticket and how it was paid for.



Table 3.2: The three variables in the probability file, 100 registration records





Variable
Categories
Count




Attendance
Attended, No_Show
83, 17


Ticket_Type
Standard, VIP
80, 20


Payment_Method
Bank_Transfer, Cash, Credit_Card
40, 30, 30







Where a probability comes from
A probability from records is one of three kinds a manager meets.

From records: 83 of 100 registered people attended, so the probability of attending is 0.83. This chapter uses records wherever they exist.
From judgement: an experienced events manager estimates that a new venue has a 0.9 chance of being ready on time. Judgement fills the gap when no records exist, and the report names it as judgement.
From equally likely outcomes: a fair die has six faces, so each has a probability of \(1/6\). Games of chance work this way. Business events rarely do.

A probability from records describes the past. It serves as a forecast when the coming event resembles the past ones: a similar audience, a similar price and a similar reminder process. When those conditions change, the probability needs fresh evidence.


A probability as a long-run share
A probability from records rests on one idea: over many repetitions, the share of cases in which an event happens settles towards its probability. A short run can stray a long way from it. The coin toss below shows the idea on a fair coin, whose probability of heads is 0.5.



If the panel above stays blank, open the probability explorer in a new tab.


Press Toss 10 three times. Each run gives a different share of heads, and some land well away from 0.50.
Press Reset, then Toss 10,000. The chart shows the share wandering over the first few hundred tosses and then settling close to 0.50.

The 100 registration records work the same way. 83 attendances in 100 give a probability of 0.83, and a file of 10 records could easily have given 0.7 or 0.9. The more records behind a probability, the closer it settles to the rate the next event will show.


The complement rule
The complement of an event is everything outside it. The complement of “attended” is “did not attend”, which the file records as No_Show. An event and its complement cover every case between them, so their probabilities add to 1.
\[P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)\]
The complement rule simplifies calculation. When an event is hard to count and its complement is easy, count the complement and subtract from 1.

Worked example 3.1

Attendance and its complement

The probability file holds 100 registration records, and 83 of them record Attended.
Calculate the probability that a registered person attends, then use the complement rule to find the probability of a no-show. State what the two figures mean for a team expecting 100 registrations.


Attendance: The question is about all registered people, so the denominator is all 100 records.
\[P(\text{Attended}) = \frac{83}{100} = 0.83\]
No-show, by the complement rule:
\[P(\text{No\_Show}) = 1 - 0.83 = 0.17\]
The file confirms it: 17 records read No_Show, and \(17 \div 100 = 0.17\).
Meaning: If the next event resembles the past ones, about 83 of every 100 registered people will attend and about 17 seats will stay empty. A team ordering food for every registration will pay for approximately 17 uneaten meals per 100 registrations. Part 2 shows how far the real number can stray from 83.









TipTry It 3.1: A training centre



A training centre had 120 registrations for its last course, and 90 people attended.

Calculate the probability that a registered person attended.
Use the complement rule to find the probability of a no-show.
The next course has 160 registrations. About how many people should the centre expect to attend, if the next course resembles the last?









NoteCheck your answer






\(P(\text{attended}) = 90 \div 120 = 0.75\).
\(P(\text{no-show}) = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25\). As a check, \(120 - 90 = 30\) people stayed away, and \(30 \div 120 = 0.25\).
\(0.75 \times 160 = 120\) people. The centre should plan for about 120 attendees, with about 40 empty seats.

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Contingency tables and joint probability
A contingency table counts the cases that fall into each combination of two categorical variables. Each row is one category of the first variable, each column is one category of the second and each cell counts the cases that belong to both. Chapter 1 called the same layout a cross-tabulation.
Table 3.3 crosses ticket type with attendance for the 100 registration records.



Table 3.3: Ticket type by attendance, 100 registration records





Ticket type
Attended
No_Show
Total




Standard
67
13
80


VIP
16
4
20


Total
83
17
100






Each number in the table answers a different question.

A cell counts the cases in two categories at once. 16 people held a VIP ticket and attended.
A row total or a column total counts one category on its own. 20 people held a VIP ticket. These totals sit in the margins of the table, so a probability calculated from one is called a marginal probability.
The grand total, 100, counts every case.

A joint probability is the probability that two events happen together. Divide a cell by the grand total:
\[P(A \text{ and } B) = \frac{\text{number of cases in both } A \text{ and } B}{\text{number of cases the question is about}}\]
For example: the probability that a registered person held a VIP ticket and attended is \(16 \div 100 = 0.16\). The marginal probability of a VIP ticket is \(20 \div 100 = 0.20\).
A joint probability is never larger than either of its marginal probabilities, because every case counted in the cell is also counted in its row and in its column. If a joint probability exceeds a marginal one, a counting error has occurred.

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Conditional probability
A conditional probability is the probability of one event among the cases where a second event has happened. The second event narrows the denominator to a subgroup. The word “given” signals it, and so do the phrases “among”, “of those who” and “within”.
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{\text{number of cases in both } A \text{ and } B}{\text{number of cases in } B} = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}\]
\(P(A \mid B)\) is read as “the probability of \(A\) given \(B\)”. The vertical bar stands for “given”.
For example: among the 20 VIP ticket holders, 16 attended.
\[P(\text{Attended} \mid \text{VIP}) = \frac{16}{20} = 0.80\]
The same figure comes from the second form of the formula: \(0.16 \div 0.20 = 0.80\).

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
The addition rule
The addition rule gives the probability that at least one of two events happens: \(A\), or \(B\), or both. Add the two probabilities, then subtract the joint probability, because the cases in both events were counted once in each.
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\]
For example: a registered person who holds a VIP ticket or paid in cash. From the file, 20 people hold a VIP ticket and 30 paid in cash. Five people did both, so adding 20 and 30 counts those 5 twice.
\[P(\text{VIP or Cash}) = 0.20 + 0.30 - 0.05 = 0.45\]
A count confirms it: \(20 + 30 - 5 = 45\) different people, out of 100.

Mutually exclusive events
Two events are mutually exclusive when no case can belong to both. Each registration record carries exactly one payment method, so “paid in cash” and “paid by credit card” are mutually exclusive. Their joint probability is 0, and the addition rule loses its last term:
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) \quad \text{when } A \text{ and } B \text{ are mutually exclusive}\]
\[P(\text{Cash or Credit\_Card}) = 0.30 + 0.30 = 0.60\]
An event and its complement are always mutually exclusive, and together they cover every case. The complement rule is the addition rule applied to that pair: \(P(A) + P(\text{not } A) = 1\).

13  Part 1: Probability from records

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Independence and the multiplication rule
Two events are independent when knowing that one has happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged. In symbols, \(A\) and \(B\) are independent when
\[P(A \mid B) = P(A)\]
Independence is an empirical claim tested by the records. Compare the conditional probability with the overall one.

Ticket type and attendance: \(P(\text{Attended}) = 0.83\). Among VIP ticket holders it is 0.80, and among Standard ticket holders it is \(67 \div 80 = 0.8375\). The three figures are close, so ticket type tells you little about whether a person attends. The two variables are close to independent.
Payment method and attendance: Among cash payers the rate falls to 0.767, against 0.83 overall. Knowing that a person paid in cash reduces the probability of attendance. Worked example 3.3 used exactly that difference.

A sample of 100 records rarely gives two exactly equal figures, even when two variables are independent in the wider population. Chapter 10’s chi-squared test decides whether a difference is larger than sampling variation. In this chapter, judge it by size and by what it would change.

The multiplication rule
The multiplication rule turns the conditional probability formula round to give a joint probability:
\[P(A \text{ and } B) = P(B) \times P(A \mid B)\]
For example: 20 per cent of registered people hold a VIP ticket, and 80 per cent of those attend. \(P(\text{VIP and Attended}) = 0.20 \times 0.80 = 0.16\), the cell value from Table 3.3.
When \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, \(P(A \mid B)\) equals \(P(A)\), and the rule becomes
\[P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B) \quad \text{when } A \text{ and } B \text{ are independent}\]
This shorter form needs independence. Used on dependent events, it gives the wrong joint probability. For cash payers who stay away, the shortcut gives \(0.30 \times 0.17 = 0.051\), about 5 people in 100, where the records hold 7.

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Probability trees
A probability tree draws two or more uncertain events in the order they happen. Each branch carries a probability. The branches at the first split carry marginal probabilities, and every later branch carries a probability conditional on the path that leads to it.
Figure 3.1 draws the registration records as a tree. The first split is ticket type, the second is attendance.






Figure 3.1: A probability tree for the 100 registration records: ticket type first, then attendance given the ticket type.



Three rules read every probability tree:

Multiply along a path. The probability of a complete path is the product of the probabilities on its branches. This is the multiplication rule: \(P(\text{Standard and Attended}) = 0.80 \times 0.8375 = 0.67\).
Add across paths. The probability of an outcome that two or more paths share is the sum of those paths. Two paths end in attendance, so \(P(\text{Attended}) = 0.67 + 0.16 = 0.83\), the figure from worked example 3.1.
Check the totals. The branches leaving any one point add to 1, and so do the path probabilities: \(0.67 + 0.13 + 0.16 + 0.04 = 1.00\).

A tree is most useful when the stages happen in sequence, and when the second stage depends on the first. Part 2 adds a second kind of point, where the manager chooses the branch, and the probability tree becomes a decision tree.

13  Part 1: Probability from records

title: Part 1: Probability from records
text:
Section summary
A decision under uncertainty follows eight steps, from the question to the recommendation, and probability supplies the numbers for steps 4 to 6. A probability from records is a count divided by the number of cases the question is about, and the complement rule gives the chance that an event does not happen. A contingency table holds joint counts in its cells and marginal counts in its margins. A conditional probability narrows the denominator to a subgroup, and reversing the condition changes the question. The addition rule subtracts the overlap that would otherwise be counted twice. Independent events leave each other’s probabilities unchanged, and the multiplication rule joins events along the paths of a probability tree.






Next: Part 2, expected value and decision trees puts payoffs on the branches and chooses between options.

13  Part 1: Probability from records

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Random variables and probability distributions
In part 1 we turned records into probabilities. In this part we assign monetary values to those probabilities, so that we can compare two options with uncertain outcomes and then estimate how many registered people will attend.
Some numbers we can only know after something uncertain has happened. For example: our events team signs a catering contract with a local vendor. We do not yet know our profit from the event, because it depends on whether the vendor delivers on time or late. Until the delivery happens, our profit could take one of two values.
A number like this is called a random variable: a number whose value is decided by chance. The number of registered people who attend an event is another random variable, since we learn its value only on the day of the event.
crumbs: Chapter 3: Decision Processes, Decision Trees, CPA/CPM, Gantt Charts, and Basics of Probability
14  Part 2: Expected value and decision trees

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Where the profit comes from
For example: imagine the event earns 20,000 USD from tickets and the local vendor charges 13,056.38 USD. If the vendor delivers on time, our profit is:
\[20{,}000 - 13{,}056.38 = 6{,}943.62 \text{ USD}\]
If the vendor delivers late, we must also buy emergency supplies, which cost 8,762.09 USD. Our costs are now greater than our income, so we make a loss:
\[20{,}000 - 13{,}056.38 - 8{,}762.09 = -1{,}818.47 \text{ USD}\]
The money we are left with at the end of each outcome is called the payoff. A positive payoff is a profit, and a negative payoff is a loss.


Probability distributions
A probability distribution lists every value a random variable can take, together with the probability of each value. For example: the local vendor delivers on time with probability 0.740 and late with probability 0.260. These probabilities come from scenario 1 of our data file, described in The vendor scenarios. So our profit has this distribution:

Each probability lies between 0 and 1.
The probabilities add to 1, because the list covers every possible value: in Table 3.9, \(0.740 + 0.260 = 1.000\).

In each scenario our events team compares two vendors for the same catering contract: a local vendor and an international vendor. 14  Part 2: Expected value and decision trees

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Expected value
When we choose a vendor, we need one figure that sums up what each contract is worth to us before we know the outcome, and the expected value gives us that figure.
For example: suppose we signed the local vendor’s contract from scenario 1 100 times. With an on-time probability of 0.740, about 74 deliveries would arrive on time, each giving a profit of 6,943.62 USD. The other 26 would arrive late, each giving a loss of 1,818.47 USD. Our total over the 100 contracts would be:
\[74 \times 6{,}943.62 - 26 \times 1{,}818.47 = 513{,}827.88 - 47{,}280.22 = 466{,}547.66 \text{ USD}\]
Shared across the 100 contracts, that is \(466{,}547.66 \div 100 = 4{,}665.48\) USD per contract. This average per contract is the expected value of the contract.
We reach the same figure in one line by multiplying each payoff by its probability and adding the results:
\[EV = 0.740 \times 6{,}943.62 + 0.260 \times (-1{,}818.47) = 5{,}138.28 - 472.80 = 4{,}665.48 \text{ USD}\]
Each payoff counts in proportion to its probability: the on-time payoff contributes 74 per cent of its value and the late payoff 26 per cent. In general, the expected value of a random variable is:
\[EV = \sum p_i \, x_i = p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 + \dots\]
where \(x_i\) is the \(i\)th possible value of the random variable (here, a payoff in USD) and \(p_i\) is the probability of that value. The symbol \(\sum\) means “add up over every outcome”. The vendor file calls an on-time delivery a success and a late delivery a failure, so for a vendor the formula has two terms:
\[EV = p_{\text{success}} \times x_{\text{success}} + p_{\text{failure}} \times x_{\text{failure}}\]
An expected value measured in money is called the expected monetary value.
On any one contract we receive one of the two payoffs, either +6,943.62 USD or −1,818.47 USD. The expected value of 4,665.48 USD lies between them, and we receive it only as an average across many contracts.

14  Part 2: Expected value and decision trees

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Risk behind the expected value
An expected value sums up a contract in one number: the average payoff over many contracts. A single contract can give a payoff far from that average, so we also need to know how far. For example: imagine that contract A gives us 5,000 USD whatever happens, while contract B gives us a profit of 15,000 USD with probability 0.5, or a loss of 5,000 USD with probability 0.5. The two contracts have the same expected value of 5,000 USD:
\[EV_B = 0.5 \times 15{,}000 + 0.5 \times (-5{,}000) = 7{,}500 - 2{,}500 = 5{,}000 \text{ USD}\]
Contract A can never lose us money, and contract B loses us 5,000 USD half the time. So before we choose, we look at three more figures in a risk review.
The probability of a loss: For a vendor, this is the probability of a late delivery.
The worst outcome: This is the largest loss we can make on the contract. We need to ask whether we can absorb that loss.
The standard deviation of the payoff: This measures how far the payoff typically falls from the expected value. It is the same measure of spread as the standard deviation in chapter 1. The difference is that each squared distance counts in proportion to its probability, just as each payoff did in the expected value:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\sum p_i \, (x_i - EV)^2}\]
For example: the local vendor in scenario 1 has an expected value of 4,665.48 USD. The on-time payoff lies \(6{,}943.62 - 4{,}665.48 = 2{,}278.14\) USD above it, and the late payoff lies \(-1{,}818.47 - 4{,}665.48 = -6{,}483.95\) USD below it. So the standard deviation is:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{0.740 \times 2{,}278.14^2 + 0.260 \times 6{,}483.95^2}\] \[= \sqrt{3{,}840{,}542 + 10{,}930{,}818} = \sqrt{14{,}771{,}360} = 3{,}843 \text{ USD}\]
When there are only two outcomes, the same answer comes from a shorter formula:
\[\sigma = (x_{\text{success}} - x_{\text{failure}}) \times \sqrt{p_{\text{success}} \, (1 - p_{\text{success}})}\]
The first bracket is the gap between the two payoffs. The late payoff is negative, so subtracting it adds its size: \(6{,}943.62 - (-1{,}818.47) = 6{,}943.62 + 1{,}818.47 = 8{,}762.09\) USD, and the standard deviation is:
\[\sigma = 8{,}762.09 \times \sqrt{0.740 \times 0.260} = 8{,}762.09 \times 0.43863 = 3{,}843 \text{ USD}\]
This is the same as the long formula. A wider gap between the two payoffs, or a probability nearer 0.5, gives a larger standard deviation.

text:
Decision trees
A decision tree sets out a decision on paper from left to right: the options we can choose from, the uncertain events that follow each option and the payoff at the end of every path. It is the probability tree from part 1 with one addition: points where we choose which branch to take.



Table 3.16: The parts of a decision tree











Part
Symbol
Meaning
In the vendor decision




Decision node
Square
A point where we choose one branch
Book the local or the international vendor


Chance node
Circle
A point where the outcome is uncertain
The vendor delivers on time or late


Branch
Line
One option, or one outcome with its probability
Late, probability 0.260


End node
Triangle
The payoff at the end of a complete path
-1,818.47 USD






We draw a tree in four steps:

Put a decision node at the left and draw one branch for each option.
At the end of each option, put a chance node and draw one branch for each outcome. Write its probability on the branch. The probabilities leaving a chance node add to 1.
At the end of each outcome, put an end node and write the payoff.
Roll the tree back from right to left, as described in Rolling back a tree, and mark the chosen branch.

In Figure 3.2, the vendor decision from worked example 3.6 is drawn as a tree.

14  Part 2: Expected value and decision trees

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Rolling back a tree
Rolling back a decision tree means working from the payoffs on the right towards the decision on the left. At each node we write a single value:

At a chance node, the value is the expected value of its branches.
At a decision node, the value is the value of the best branch, the one with the largest value. We strike through the branches we reject, as in Figure 3.2, where the rejected branch carries two short strokes.

In a one-stage tree, such as the vendor tree, rolling back is the expected value calculation from worked example 3.6. Rolling back is more useful when we face a second decision after a chance event. For example: we book an outdoor venue, and if it rains we must decide on the day whether to move indoors. We can only value the outdoor venue once we know what we would do in the rain, so we make the later decision first and work back to the first one.

Worked example 3.8

An outdoor venue with a fallback

In this illustrative example, separate from the data files, we can book an indoor hall for a guaranteed profit of 8,000 USD, or an outdoor venue. Outdoors, good weather (probability 0.7) gives a profit of 12,000 USD. In bad weather (probability 0.3) we decide on the day: move indoors at short notice for a profit of 4,000 USD, or stay outdoors and make a loss of 2,000 USD.
Draw the tree, roll it back and choose a venue. Then calculate how much the possibility of moving indoors is worth to us.


The tree: In Figure 3.3, the decision node at the left is the choice of venue, the chance node after “Outdoor venue” is the weather and a second decision node follows bad weather.






Figure 3.3: The outdoor venue decision, a two-stage tree rolled back from right to left.



Step 1, the later decision: In bad weather, moving indoors gives a profit of 4,000 USD and staying outdoors gives a loss of 2,000 USD. We would move indoors, so we write 4,000 USD on the bad-weather decision node.
Step 2, the chance node:
\[EV_{\text{outdoor}} = 0.7 \times 12{,}000 + 0.3 \times 4{,}000\] \[= 8{,}400 + 1{,}200 = 9{,}600 \text{ USD}\]
Step 3, the first decision: The outdoor venue’s 9,600 USD exceeds the hall’s 8,000 USD, so we book the outdoor venue.
The value of the fallback: Suppose moving indoors were impossible, so we had to stay outdoors in bad weather.
\[EV = 0.7 \times 12{,}000 + 0.3 \times (-2{,}000)\] \[= 8{,}400 - 600 = 7{,}800 \text{ USD}\]
That is less than the hall’s 8,000 USD, so without the fallback we would book the hall. Being able to move indoors is worth \(9{,}600 - 7{,}800 = 1{,}800\) USD to us in expected value. When we negotiate the outdoor booking, we should secure that fallback in writing before signing.









TipTry It 3.6: Bid or settle



In this illustrative example, we can sign a fixed contract now for a profit of 6,000 USD, or bid for a conference contract. A winning bid (probability 0.4) brings a profit of 15,000 USD. If the bid fails (probability 0.6), we decide again: take a smaller fixed contract for 3,000 USD, or take nothing for 0 USD.

Draw the decision tree.
Roll it back and choose between bidding and signing now.
State the probability that we end up with less than the 6,000 USD we could have signed for.









NoteCheck your answer






A decision node with two branches: “Sign now”, ending at 6,000 USD, and “Bid”, leading to a chance node. From the chance node, “Win 0.4” ends at 15,000 USD and “Lose 0.6” leads to a second decision node with “Smaller contract”, 3,000 USD, and “Nothing”, 0 USD.
The later decision: 3,000 exceeds 0, so take the smaller contract. At the chance node, \(0.4 \times 15{,}000 + 0.6 \times 3{,}000 = 6{,}000 + 1{,}800 = 7{,}800\) USD. Bidding, at 7,800 USD, exceeds signing now at 6,000 USD, so bid.
We end with less than 6,000 USD whenever the bid fails, probability 0.6. The bid has the higher expected value and a higher probability of an outcome below 6,000 USD, and a recommendation needs to report both.

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Counting successes: the binomial model
Now we return to our first question: how many registered people will attend? Each registration has two outcomes, attend or stay away, and an event has many registrations. The binomial model gives the probability distribution of the number of successes in a fixed number of trials. Here a trial is one registration, and a success is a person who attends. The model applies when four conditions hold:

There is a fixed number of trials, \(n\): here, the registrations.
Each trial has two outcomes, success or failure: here, attended or no-show.
The probability of success, \(p\), is the same for every trial: here, 0.83 from the records.
The trials are independent: whether one person attends has no effect on whether another attends.

The fourth condition needs checking every time we use the model. For example: colleagues who registered as a group travel together, so they tend to attend or stay away together. Group bookings break independence, and attendance then varies more than the model predicts.

Where the binomial probabilities come from
We can see where the model comes from by drawing a probability tree. Take three registrations, each attending with probability 0.83. The tree has \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\) paths, and because the registrations are independent, we multiply the probabilities along each path. Three of the paths have exactly two people attending, because the one person who stays away can be the first, the second or the third. Each of those paths has probability \(0.83 \times 0.83 \times 0.17\).



Table 3.17: The binomial distribution for 3 registrations, each attending with probability 0.83

The general formula multiplies the number of paths by the probability of one path. The number of paths with exactly \(k\) successes is written \(\binom{n}{k}\) and read “n choose k”. For example: with three registrations and two attending, \(\binom{3}{2} = 3\), as in Table 3.17.
\[P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} \, p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}\]
where \(X\) is the number of successes, \(n\) the number of trials, \(k\) the number of successes you want the probability of, and \(p\) the probability of success on one trial.
We rarely calculate it by hand, because a spreadsheet does it in one function: =BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, FALSE) gives \(P(X = k)\), and =BINOM.DIST(k, n, p, TRUE) gives the probability of \(k\) or fewer.


The mean and standard deviation of a binomial
The expected number of successes and its standard deviation have short formulas:
\[\mu = n \, p \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{n \, p \, (1 - p)}\]
where \(\mu\) (the Greek letter mu) is the expected number of successes and \(\sigma\) is its standard deviation.
For the three registrations, \(\mu = 3 \times 0.83 = 2.49\), and the expected value formula from earlier in this part gives the same figure: \(3 \times 0.5718 + 2 \times 0.3513 + 1 \times 0.0720 + 0 \times 0.0049 = 2.49\).
When \(n p\) and \(n (1 - p)\) are both at least 10, the binomial distribution has close to a normal shape. We can then estimate its probabilities with the z-scores and the normal table from chapter 2. The binomial counts whole people, and the normal model treats attendance as a smooth scale. So when we turn a count into a boundary, we move it by half a person: “more than 105” means 106 or more, so its boundary on the smooth scale is 105.5.

Worked example 3.9

Is the room big enough?

The next event has 120 registrations and the room seats 105. Each registered person attends with probability 0.83, independently of the others.
Calculate the expected attendance and its standard deviation, then estimate the probability that more than 105 people attend. Decide whether we should move to a larger room.


Check the conditions: There are 120 fixed registrations with two outcomes each, the same probability from the records, and we assume independence. \(n p = 99.6\) and \(n (1 - p) = 20.4\), both at least 10, so the normal model applies.
Mean and standard deviation:
\[\mu = 120 \times 0.83 = 99.6\] \[\sigma = \sqrt{120 \times 0.83 \times 0.17} = \sqrt{16.932} = 4.115\]
More than 105: The count “more than 105” begins at 106, so the boundary is 105.5.
\[z = \frac{105.5 - 99.6}{4.115} = \frac{5.9}{4.115} = 1.43\]
The standard normal table gives an area above 1.43 of 0.0764. The spreadsheet’s exact figure, =1-BINOM.DIST(105, 120, 0.83, TRUE), is 0.0710.
Decision: About 7 events in 100 with this registration pattern would have more people than seats. We need to decide whether a 1 in 14 probability of turning people away is acceptable. If a larger room costs little, we should take it. If it is expensive, a waiting list and a reminder to confirm attendance a week ahead would manage the risk at lower cost.









TipTry It 3.7: Catering for 150



An event has 150 registrations, each attending with probability 0.83. The caterer needs a firm order of 130 meals.

Calculate the expected attendance and its standard deviation.
Estimate the probability that more than 130 people attend, using the normal model.

NoteCheck your answer






\(\mu = 150 \times 0.83 = 124.5\). \(\sigma = \sqrt{150 \times 0.83 \times 0.17} = \sqrt{21.165} = 4.601\).
With the boundary at 130.5, \(z = (130.5 - 124.5) \div 4.601 = 6.0 \div 4.601 = 1.30\). The area above 1.30 is 0.0968, about 10 per cent.
=1-BINOM.DIST(130, 150, 0.83, TRUE), which returns 0.0927.
130 meals covers the expected 124.5 attendees with 5 or 6 to spare, and falls short in about 1 event in 10. For a buffet with some flexibility this is defensible. For a seated dinner we may want a few more meals or a late top-up arrangement with the caterer.

title: Part 2: Expected value and decision trees
text:
Section summary
A random variable is a number whose value is decided by chance, and its probability distribution lists every value with its probability. The expected value counts each value in proportion to its probability, and it gives the average payoff over many repeats of the same decision. A risk review sets the probability of a loss, the worst outcome and the standard deviation beside the expected value. A decision tree draws decisions as squares, chance events as circles and payoffs as triangles, and rolling it back from right to left identifies the option with the highest expected value. In the vendor scenario file, the international vendor has the higher expected value in all 50 scenarios and the larger loss in 49, so our choice depends on the loss we can absorb. The binomial model counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials, with mean \(n p\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{n p (1 - p)}\).






Next: In part 3, project time, we turn from money to days and find the tasks that set the date of the event.

title: Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts
text:
Projects as linked tasks
In parts 1 and 2 we evaluated uncertain outcomes in money. In this part we evaluate them in time: we calculate how long preparation will take, identify the tasks that set the completion date and calculate the probability of meeting a deadline.
A project is a set of tasks that together produce one result, such as an event, by a fixed date. Some tasks can start at once. Others must wait for earlier tasks to finish. A task that must finish before another can start is that task’s predecessor.
Two names cover the same method. Critical path analysis (CPA) is the usual name in the UK, and the critical path method (CPM) is the usual name in the United States. In this chapter we use the abbreviation CPM.
The CPM file, Week3_CPM_Task_Data.csv, lists the 8 tasks we must finish before the event. Each row gives three estimates of the task’s duration in working days, explained in Three-point estimates and PERT, and the task’s predecessors. To keep Table 3.18 narrow, the predecessors of Staff_Briefing are given by their IDs: “3, 4, 5 and 6” means tasks 3, 4, 5 and 6.
In Figure 3.4 the tasks are drawn as a network. Each box is a task, and each arrow runs from a predecessor to the task that waits for it. Reading the arrows from left to right gives the order of work. The figure also marks two results you will calculate later in this part: the slack of each task and the critical path.
One link in the network adds nothing. Staff_Briefing lists Catering_Arrangement as a predecessor, but the briefing also waits for AV_and_Equipment_Setup, which itself starts only once catering has finished. So the briefing can never start before catering ends, and the direct link from catering to the briefing is redundant. In the figure it is drawn as a dotted arrow. To find a redundant link, read the network and the table together.

title: Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts
text:
Three-point estimates and PERT
A task duration is uncertain, just as a vendor’s delivery time is. The programme evaluation and review technique (PERT) asks the people who know each task for three estimates:

Optimistic, \(O\): the duration if everything goes well
Most likely, \(M\): the usual duration
Pessimistic, \(P\): the duration if things go badly, short of disaster

PERT combines them into an expected duration, \(T_E\). This is a weighted average: the most likely estimate counts four times as much as each of the other two.
\[T_E = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6}\]
We divide by 6 because the weights add to \(1 + 4 + 1 = 6\). PERT also gives each task a variance, which measures how uncertain its duration is. PERT assumes that the range from the optimistic to the pessimistic estimate covers about six standard deviations, so one standard deviation is one sixth of that range:
\[\sigma = \frac{P - O}{6} \qquad \sigma^2 = \left(\frac{P - O}{6}\right)^2\]
A task with a wide gap between its optimistic and pessimistic estimates has a large variance, and a task whose estimates sit close together has a small variance.

Worked example 3.10

The expected duration of the venue booking

The venue booking takes 2 days at best, 5 days most likely and 6 days at worst.
Calculate its PERT expected duration, standard deviation and variance. Explain why the expected duration falls below the most likely estimate.


Expected duration:
\[T_E = \frac{2 + 4 \times 5 + 6}{6}\] \[= \frac{2 + 20 + 6}{6} = \frac{28}{6} = 4.667 \text{ days}\]
Standard deviation and variance:
\[\sigma = \frac{6 - 2}{6} = 0.667 \text{ days}\] \[\sigma^2 = \left(\frac{4}{6}\right)^2 = \frac{16}{36} = 0.444\]
Why it falls below 5: The optimistic estimate sits 3 days below the most likely one, and the pessimistic estimate only 1 day above it. So the estimates lean towards an early finish, and the average falls below 5. When the pessimistic estimate sits far above the most likely one, the opposite happens and the expected duration is above the most likely estimate.

title: Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts
text:
The forward pass
The forward pass works through the network from left to right and finds the earliest time each task can start and finish. We count time in days from the start of the project, so time 0 is the start of day 1, and time 5 is the end of day 5.

Earliest start, ES: a task with no predecessors starts at 0. A task with predecessors starts when the last of them finishes, so its ES is the largest EF among its predecessors.
Earliest finish, EF: the earliest start plus the duration.

\[EF = ES + \text{duration}\]
The project’s earliest finishing time is the largest EF of all its tasks.
crumbs: Chapter 3: Decision Processes, Decision Trees, CPA/CPM, Gantt Charts, and Basics of Probability
15  Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts

title: Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts
section: The backward pass and the critical path
text:
The backward pass and the critical path
The backward pass works from right to left and finds the latest time each task can start and finish without delaying the project.

Latest finish, LF: a task with no successors finishes at the project’s finishing time. A task with successors must finish before the first of them has to start, so its LF is the smallest LS among its successors.
Latest start, LS: the latest finish minus the duration.

\[LS = LF - \text{duration}\]
The gap between the two passes is the task’s slack, also called float: the number of days the task can be delayed without moving the project’s finishing date.
\[\text{Slack} = LS - ES = LF - EF\]
A task with zero slack is a critical task. The chain of critical tasks from the start of the project to its end is the critical path. Its total duration is the project’s finishing time, because it is the longest chain of linked tasks in the network. Any delay to a critical task delays the entire project.

Worked example 3.11

The critical path for the event

Use the most likely durations from Table 3.18 and the predecessors shown there.
Run the forward and backward passes, calculate each task’s slack and name the critical path and the project’s finishing day.


Forward pass, left to right:

Venue_Booking and Speaker_Confirmation have no predecessors, so each starts at 0. They finish at \(0 + 5 = 5\) and \(0 + 3 = 3\).
Marketing_Launch and Catering_Arrangement each wait for the venue: ES 5, EF \(5 + 5 = 10\) and \(5 + 4 = 9\).
Registration_System_Setup waits for the speakers: ES 3, EF \(3 + 5 = 8\).
AV_and_Equipment_Setup waits for catering: ES 9, EF \(9 + 5 = 14\).
Staff_Briefing waits for four tasks, finishing at 10, 8, 9 and 14. It starts at the largest, 14, and finishes at 15.
Final_Rehearsal: ES 15 and EF 16, so the project finishes at 16.

Backward pass, right to left:

Final_Rehearsal has LF 16 and LS \(16 - 1 = 15\), so Staff_Briefing has LF 15 and LS 14.
AV_and_Equipment_Setup, Marketing_Launch and Registration_System_Setup each feed only the briefing, so each has LF 14. Their LS values are \(14 - 5 = 9\), \(14 - 5 = 9\) and \(14 - 5 = 9\).
Catering_Arrangement feeds the AV setup (LS 9) and the briefing (LS 14). Take the smaller: LF 9, LS \(9 - 4 = 5\).
Venue_Booking feeds marketing (LS 9) and catering (LS 5), so its LF is 5 and its LS is 0.
Speaker_Confirmation feeds registration (LS 9), so its LF is 9 and its LS is \(9 - 3 = 6\).

section: The probability of meeting a deadline
text:
The probability of meeting a deadline
With PERT, each task’s duration is uncertain, so the finishing date is a random variable. We can then use the normal model from chapter 2 to estimate the probability of meeting a deadline, in three steps:

Mean of the path: Add the expected durations along the critical path: here, 16.0 days.
Variance of the path: Add the variances of the tasks on the critical path. This assumes the task durations are independent of one another.
Probability: Treat the path’s duration as normal, find the z-score of the deadline and read the area below it from the standard normal table.

\[\sigma^2_{\text{path}} = \sum \sigma^2_{\text{task}} \qquad z = \frac{\text{deadline} - T_{\text{path}}}{\sigma_{\text{path}}}\]
where \(T_{\text{path}}\) is the expected length of the critical path and \(\sigma_{\text{path}}\) is the square root of its variance.
Variances add along a path, so to get the standard deviation of the path, add the variances first and then take the square root of the total.

Worked example 3.12

Ready in 18 working days?

The venue manager asks us to confirm that the event will be ready within 18 working days of the start of planning.
Calculate the variance and standard deviation of the critical path from Table 3.19, and estimate the probability of finishing within 18 days. State the limits of the estimate.


Variance of the path: Add the five critical tasks’ variances. Each is a whole number of 36ths, because it is a difference divided by 6 and then squared: 0.444 is \(16/36\) and 0.028 is \(1/36\). Adding the fractions avoids rounding error.
\[\sigma^2_{\text{path}} = \frac{16 + 16 + 16 + 1 + 1}{36} = \frac{50}{36} = 1.389\]
Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\text{path}} = \sqrt{1.389} = 1.18\) days.
z-score of the deadline:
\[z = \frac{18 - 16.0}{1.18} = \frac{2.0}{1.18} = 1.70\]
The standard normal table gives an area of 0.9554 below 1.70.
Answer: The event has a probability of about 0.96 of being ready within 18 working days. If we promise 18 days, we will miss the deadline about once in 22 projects.
Limits: The estimate assumes the five task durations are independent. A single cause, such as a staff shortage, can delay three tasks simultaneously. It assumes the duration of a five-task path follows a normal distribution, which is an approximation. It also ignores the other paths. The next-longest path, through marketing, is expected to take 11.8 days. It is therefore highly unlikely to exceed the duration of the critical path. In a project where two paths have similar durations, the true risk is higher than this method calculates.









TipTry It 3.10: Choosing a promise



Use the critical path figures from worked example 3.12: a mean of 16.0 days and a standard deviation of 1.18 days.

Estimate the probability of finishing within 17 days.
Estimate the probability of finishing within 15 days.
The venue manager wants a date we will meet 95 times in 100. Which day should we promise?









NoteCheck your answer






\(z = (17 - 16.0) \div 1.18 = 0.85\). The area below 0.85 is 0.8023, about 80 per cent.
\(z = (15 - 16.0) \div 1.18 = -0.85\). The area below \(-0.85\) is \(1 - 0.8023 = 0.1977\), about 20 per cent.
The 95th percentile has \(z = 1.645\), which gives \(16.0 + 1.645 \times 1.18 = 16.0 + 1.94 = 17.94\) days, so promise 18 working days.

title: Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts
text:
Gantt charts
A Gantt chart is a project schedule drawn as horizontal bars against a calendar. Each task has its own row, and its bar runs from its start day to its finish day. You can see at a glance which tasks run at the same time, who is responsible for each and when the project ends. From the network diagram we read the order of the tasks, and from the Gantt chart we read their dates.
The Gantt file, Week3_Gantt_Data.csv, holds our schedule. It gives each task a start day, a duration, an end day, the team responsible and a flag for the critical path. The schedule is drawn in Figure 3.5.






Figure 3.5: The events team’s schedule as a Gantt chart, drawn from the Gantt file.




Day numbers and CPM times
In the Gantt file, days are numbered from 1. In CPM, time is counted from 0. A task with ES 0 and EF 5 occupies days 1 to 5. Two rules convert one to the other:
\[\text{Start day} = ES + 1 \qquad \text{End day} = EF\]
For example: catering has ES 5 and EF 9 in Table 3.20, so it runs from day 6 to day 9.


Reading and checking a Gantt chart
A Gantt chart may appear complete once the bars are drawn. Before you use it to manage the project, check it against the network with the five checks in Table 3.21, which cover most errors.



Table 3.21: Five checks for a Gantt chart










Check
Question
In Figure 3.5




Order
Does every task start after all its predecessors end?
Staff_Briefing starts on day 15, after the last predecessor ends on day 14


Dates
Does every bar match ES + 1 and EF from the CPM?
All 8 tasks match Table 3.20


Critical path
Are the zero-slack tasks marked, and only those?
The 5 tasks flagged critical are the 5 with zero slack


Workload
Does any team carry two tasks at once?
Operations runs the venue on days 1 to 5 and catering on days 6 to 9, one after the other


Slack
Does the chart show how much each task can be delayed?
The bars sit at their earliest starts, so marketing’s 4 days of slack are invisible






In the slack check we find a limitation of the chart. A Gantt chart drawn from earliest starts shows when work can begin and leaves out how late each task could begin. Some teams draw the slack as a thin line after each bar. Others state it beside the chart.

Worked example 3.13

Moving a task inside its slack

The marketing team is occupied until day 8 and asks to start the marketing launch on day 9, three days after its planned start on day 6.
Using Table 3.20 and Figure 3.5, decide whether the request delays the event, and state how the Gantt chart changes.


The slack: Marketing_Launch has ES 5 and LS 9, so it can start as late as time 9, which is day 10, with no effect on the finishing date. Day 9 is time 8, which uses 3 of the 4 days of slack.
The new dates: Starting on day 9, the 5-day task runs to day 13. The staff briefing starts on day 15, so marketing still ends a day before it is needed.
Decision: Approve the request, because the event will still finish on day 16.
The chart: Move the marketing bar to days 9 to 13. Marketing now has 1 day of slack remaining. Note on the chart that a further delay of more than 1 day will delay the briefing.

title: Part 3: Project time, the critical path and Gantt charts
text:
Section summary
A project is a network of tasks linked by predecessors. PERT turns three estimates into an expected duration, \((O + 4M + P)/6\), and a variance, \(((P - O)/6)^2\). The forward pass finds each task’s earliest start and finish, taking the largest finish among its predecessors. The backward pass finds the latest start and finish, taking the smallest start among its successors. Slack is the gap between the two, and the tasks with zero slack form the critical path, which sets the finishing date: 16 days for our event. Adding the variances along the critical path and applying chapter 2’s normal model gives the probability of meeting a deadline. A Gantt chart is the schedule drawn on a calendar, and you need to check it against the network before you rely on it.






Next: Running the analysis, and chapter reference sets out the spreadsheet formulas, how to report each result and the key terms and formulae for the chapter.

title: Running the analysis, and chapter reference
text:
Reporting the result
Each tool in this chapter produces a numerical result that a manager must translate into a descriptive statement. An effective statement specifies the figure, its source, its interpretation and the recommended action.
For a probability: State the denominator in words so the reader knows which group the figure describes.

Among the 30 registered people who paid in cash, 23 attended, a rate of 77 per cent against 83 per cent overall. Cash payers will receive a reminder message three days before the event.

For an expected value: Provide the expected values, followed by the worst outcome and its probability, and finally the recommended choice and its condition.

Booking the international vendor gives an expected profit of 9,128 USD, against 4,665 USD for the local vendor. The international vendor delivers late about once in 6 contracts, and a late delivery costs 2,299 USD. That loss is within the team’s reserves, so the international vendor is recommended.

For attendance: Provide the expected number and the relevant risk regarding room capacity or catering orders.

Of the 120 people registered, about 100 are expected to attend. The room seats 105, and the chance that more than 105 attend is about 7 per cent, so a waiting list will be kept.

For a schedule: State the finishing date, the critical tasks and the probability of meeting the deadline.

Preparation takes 16 working days. The venue booking, catering, AV setup, staff briefing and final rehearsal are critical, and any delay to them delays the event. The team has about a 96 per cent chance of being ready within 18 working days, and 18 is the date to promise the venue.


The decision note
The decision note in the tutorial integrates all three tools. Write it in four parts:

The recommendation, in the first sentence.
The evidence, one figure per tool, each with its denominator or its source file.
The risk, the one outcome most likely to hurt, with its probability.
The action, what the team does next and by when.

Round probabilities to two decimal places or to whole percentages, money to the nearest dollar and durations to one decimal place. Cite the source file for each figure to allow verification by another analyst.

title: Running the analysis, and chapter reference
text:
Chapter review
A probability from records is a count divided by the total number of relevant cases, and the question phrasing determines the appropriate denominator. Joint probabilities occupy the cells of a contingency table, marginal probabilities appear in the margins and conditional probabilities restrict the denominator to a single row or column. The addition rule prevents double counting, while the multiplication rule links events along a probability tree. An expected value weights each payoff by its probability, and a risk review evaluates the probability of a loss, the worst outcome and the standard deviation alongside the expected value. A decision tree rolled back from right to left identifies the optimal option, while subsequent decisions can alter earlier choices. The binomial model counts successes among independent trials. PERT converts three estimates into an expected duration and a variance. The forward and backward passes calculate the slack and the critical path, and the variance of the path provides the probability of meeting a deadline. A Gantt chart displays the schedule on a calendar and requires verification against the network.

title: Running the analysis, and chapter reference
text:
Key terms
Every term links to its defining section, and the three groups correspond to the three parts of the chapter, making this section function as a revision guide.

Part 1, probability from records


Decision under uncertainty

a choice made before its outcome is known

Probability

a number from 0 to 1 stating how likely an event is

Event

an outcome that can be counted in the records

Complement

everything outside an event, with probability \(1 - P(A)\)

Contingency table

counts of cases in each combination of two categorical variables

Joint probability

the probability that two events occur together

Marginal probability

the probability of one event, from a table’s margin

Conditional probability

the probability of one event among the cases of another

Addition rule

\(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\)

Mutually exclusive

unable to occur in the same case

Independent events

events where the occurrence of one does not alter the probability of the other

Multiplication rule

\(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(B) \times P(A \mid B)\)

Probability tree

a diagram of events in the order they occur, with a probability on each branch





Part 2, expected value and decision trees


Random variable

a quantity whose value depends on an uncertain event

Probability distribution

every value of a random variable, with its probability

Expected value

the probability-weighted average of the possible values

Expected monetary value

an expected value measured in money

Risk review

the probability of a loss, the worst outcome and the spread, evaluated alongside the expected value

Decision tree

a diagram of options, chance events and payoffs

Decision node

a square, where the manager selects a branch

Chance node

a circle, where an uncertain event determines the outcome

Rolling back

calculating the value of a tree from the payoffs back to the first decision

Binomial model

the distribution of successes in \(n\) independent trials with the same \(p\)





Part 3, project time


Predecessor

a task that must finish before another can start

Critical path method (CPM)

scheduling by the longest chain of linked tasks, also called critical path analysis (CPA)

PERT

an expected duration and variance from three estimates

Forward pass

finding the earliest start and finish of each task

Backward pass

finding the latest start and finish of each task

Slack

the number of days a task can be delayed without delaying project completion, also called float

Critical path

the chain of zero-slack tasks that determines the finishing date

Gantt chart

a schedule drawn as bars against a calendar

Formula




Probability from records
\(P(A) = \dfrac{\text{cases in } A}{\text{cases the question is about}}\)


Complement
\(P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)\)


Conditional probability
\(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}\)


Addition rule
\(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\)


Mutually exclusive events
\(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\)


Multiplication rule
\(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(B) \times P(A \mid B)\)


Independent events
\(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\), so \(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)\)


Expected value
\(EV = \sum p \, x\)


Standard deviation of a payoff
\(\sigma = \sqrt{\sum p \, (x - EV)^2}\)


Two-outcome shortcut
\(\sigma = (x_{\text{success}} - x_{\text{failure}}) \sqrt{p(1 - p)}\)


Binomial probability
\(P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}\)


Binomial mean and SD
\(\mu = n p\), \(\sigma = \sqrt{n p (1 - p)}\)


PERT expected duration
\(T_E = \dfrac{O + 4M + P}{6}\)


PERT variance
\(\sigma^2 = \left(\dfrac{P - O}{6}\right)^2\)


Forward pass
\(EF = ES + \text{duration}\), ES is the largest EF of the predecessors


Backward pass
\(LS = LF - \text{duration}\), LF is the smallest LS of the successors


Slack
\(LS - ES\)


Deadline z-score
\(z = \dfrac{\text{deadline} - T_{\text{path}}}{\sqrt{\sum \sigma^2_{\text{task}}}}\)


Gantt day numbers
start day \(= ES + 1\), end day \(= EF\)

title: Tutorial: Decision trees, CPA/CPM, and Gantt practice
text:
What good looks like

Book the international vendor for scenario 20 and promise the venue 18 working days. The international vendor’s expected profit is 7,255 USD, against 3,487 USD for the local vendor. It delivers late about once in 5 contracts, and a late delivery results in a loss of 2,128 USD, which is within our reserves. Past records show 83 per cent of registered people attend, falling to 77 per cent among cash payers. Preparation takes 16 days along the critical path: venue, catering, AV setup, briefing and rehearsal. Venue, catering and AV setup each have a 4-day spread between best and worst estimates. There is about a 96 per cent chance of being ready within 18 days. Confirm the AV contractor’s dates this week and send cash payers a reminder three days before the event.

The example contains 133 words and remains within the 150-word limit. A specific sentence fulfils each of the four requirements:

“Book the international vendor for scenario 20 and promise the venue 18 working days” opens with both recommendations.
“The international vendor’s expected profit is 7,255 USD, against 3,487 USD”, “83 per cent of registered people attend” and “16 days along the critical path” give one figure from each tool.
“a late delivery results in a loss of 2,128 USD” and “about a 96 per cent chance of being ready” name the risks with their probabilities.
“Confirm the AV contractor’s dates this week and send cash payers a reminder three days before the event” ends with actions and dates.

Every figure in the note comes from the four files. You can locate each one in the workbook you built in activities 1 to 3.
