19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
One mean, one benchmark
Our question compares the spending of our customers with the figure in the marketing plan. The file DMM_Teaching_Data_Full.csv records each customer’s spending in the column Spending, in USD. Across the 200 customers:



Table 4.1: Spending in the teaching dataset





Customers, \(n\)
Mean spending, \(\bar{x}\)
Standard deviation, \(s\)




200
505.65 USD
256.84 USD






where \(n\) is the number of customers, \(\bar{x}\) (read “x-bar”) is their mean spending, and \(s\) is the standard deviation of their spending, all from chapter 1.
The plan assumed 450 USD a customer. Our customers spent \(505.65 - 450 = 55.65\) USD more than that on average. Before we tell the marketing team that the plan underestimated spending, we need to know whether the gap would still be there with a different set of 200 customers. A gap of this size could also come from the particular customers who happen to be in our file. The rest of this part builds the tool that separates the two explanations.
crumbs: Chapter 4: Single-sample Tests
19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
Sampling variation
In chapter 1 we met the difference between a population and a sample (population and sample). Our 200 customers are a sample. The population is every customer the company serves or will serve, and the marketing plan is a claim about that population.
For example: we draw 30 customers at random from our 200 and calculate their mean spending. Then we put them back and draw another 30, five times in all:



Table 4.2: Mean spending in five random samples of 30 customers





Sample
1
2
3
4
5




Mean spending, USD
590.07
495.94
520.23
532.32
548.12






All five samples come from the same 200 customers, yet the five means differ. The highest and lowest are \(590.07 - 495.94 = 94.13\) USD apart. The gap comes only from which 30 customers each sample happened to contain. This movement of a statistic from one sample to the next is called sampling variation.
Table 4.2 shows the problem. Two samples of the same customers can differ by more than the 55.65 USD gap between our mean and the plan. So we need to measure how large a gap sampling variation usually produces, and compare our gap with that measure.

The standard error of a mean
In chapter 2 we used the standard error of skewness (skewness against its standard error). A sample mean has a standard error too. The standard error of the mean measures how far a sample mean typically lies from the population mean, because of sampling variation alone:
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where \(SE_{\bar{x}}\) is the standard error of the mean, \(s\) is the standard deviation of the sample, and \(n\) is the number of cases in it.
For example: for a sample of 30 customers, the standard error is \(256.84 \div \sqrt{30}\), which is \(256.84 \div 5.477 = 46.89\) USD. That is the typical distance of each mean in Table 4.2 from the mean of all 200, 505.65 USD. For the full sample of 200, it is:
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{256.84}{\sqrt{200}} = \frac{256.84}{14.142} = 18.16 \text{ USD}\]
A larger sample gives a smaller standard error, because \(\sqrt{n}\) sits in the denominator. We know the mean of 200 customers to within about 18 USD, and the mean of 30 customers to within about 47 USD.
crumbs: Chapter 4: Single-sample Tests
19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
Stating the hypotheses
Before we look at any test result, we write our question as two competing statements about the population.
For example: either the population mean spending equals the plan’s 450 USD, or it differs from it. In symbols:
\[H_0: \mu = 450\] \[H_1: \mu \neq 450\]
where \(\mu\) (the Greek letter mu) is the mean spending of all customers in the population, and \(\neq\) means “is different from”. The benchmark in the hypotheses, here 450, is written \(\mu_0\) (“mu-nought”).
The first statement, \(H_0\), is the null hypothesis: the claim of no difference from the benchmark. The second, \(H_1\), is the alternative hypothesis: the claim that a difference exists. In a test we begin by assuming the null hypothesis is true, and then we ask how surprising our sample would be under that assumption.
Our alternative uses \(\neq\), so it allows a difference in either direction. This is a two-sided alternative, and every t-test in this book uses one. We use a two-sided alternative because we decided to test the plan before we knew whether customers spent more or less.
crumbs: Chapter 4: Single-sample Tests
19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
The t statistic
To compare our gap with the gap sampling variation produces, we divide one by the other.
For example: our gap is 55.65 USD, and the standard error is 18.16 USD. The gap is \(55.65 \div 18.16 = 3.06\) standard errors. In chapter 2 we read a z-score beyond 2 as unusual (z-scores), and the same reading applies here: a gap of three standard errors would be unusual if the plan were right.
This ratio is called the t statistic. For one mean against a benchmark it is:
\[t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{SE_{\bar{x}}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean, \(\mu_0\) is the benchmark from \(H_0\), and \(SE_{\bar{x}}\) is the standard error of the mean.
Each t statistic comes with its degrees of freedom, written \(df\). For one sample, \(df = n - 1\), so for our 200 customers \(df = 199\). JASP reports the degrees of freedom beside every t statistic, and an APA report gives them in brackets: \(t(199)\).

Worked example 4.1

Spending against the marketing plan

Use the figures in Table 4.1: 200 customers with a mean spending of 505.65 USD and a standard deviation of 256.84 USD. The marketing plan assumed 450 USD a customer.
State the hypotheses, then calculate the standard error, the t statistic and the degrees of freedom.


Step 1, the hypotheses: \(H_0: \mu = 450\) and \(H_1: \mu \neq 450\).
Step 2, the standard error:
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{256.84}{\sqrt{200}} = \frac{256.84}{14.142} = 18.16 \text{ USD}\]
Step 3, the t statistic:
\[t = \frac{505.65 - 450}{18.16} = \frac{55.65}{18.16} = 3.06\]
Step 4, the degrees of freedom: \(df = 200 - 1 = 199\).
Our mean lies 3.06 standard errors above the plan’s figure. JASP reports \(t(199) = 3.064\) from the unrounded figures.









TipTry It 4.1: Waiting time against a service standard



The company promises customers a mean wait of 45 minutes. In the column Waiting_Time_Mins, the 200 customers waited a mean of 45.455 minutes, with a standard deviation of 11.905 minutes.

State the null and alternative hypotheses.
Calculate the standard error of the mean, to three decimal places.
Calculate the t statistic and its degrees of freedom.









NoteCheck your answer






\(H_0: \mu = 45\) and \(H_1: \mu \neq 45\), where \(\mu\) is the mean waiting time of all customers.
\(SE_{\bar{x}} = 11.905 \div \sqrt{200} = 11.905 \div 14.142 = 0.842\) minutes.
\(t = (45.455 - 45) \div 0.842 = 0.455 \div 0.842 = 0.54\), with \(df = 200 - 1 = 199\).

The mean wait is about half a standard error above the promise, a gap that sampling variation produces often.
crumbs: Chapter 4: Single-sample Tests
19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
The p-value
A t statistic of 3.06 looks large, but to decide we need a probability. We find it by asking how often a t statistic this far from zero would arise if the null hypothesis were true.
For example: suppose the plan is right and the population mean is 450 USD. Then samples of 200 customers give means scattered around 450, and their t statistics are scattered around zero. Most lie between \(-2\) and \(+2\). A t statistic of 3.06 or beyond, in either direction, arises in about 2 samples in every 1,000.
This probability is the p-value: the probability of a result at least as far from the null hypothesis as ours, if the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value means our result would be rare under the null hypothesis. A large p-value means results like ours are common under it.
JASP finds the p-value from the t distribution, a symmetric curve shaped like the normal curve from chapter 2 with slightly heavier tails. Its exact shape depends on the degrees of freedom, and with \(df = 199\) it is almost identical to the standard normal curve. The p-value is the area in both tails beyond \(t = -3.06\) and \(t = +3.06\). For our spending test, JASP reports \(p = .002\).
A p-value is a probability about the data, calculated on the assumption that \(H_0\) is true. “\(p = .002\)” means that a gap this large would arise in about 2 samples in 1,000 if the plan were right. The probability that \(H_0\) itself is true is a separate quantity, and a test leaves it open.
crumbs: Chapter 4: Single-sample Tests
19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
Making the decision
Before we run a test, we choose a threshold for the p-value. This threshold is the significance level, written \(\alpha\) (alpha). Business and social science research usually sets \(\alpha = .05\), and so does this book.
The decision rule has two branches:

If \(p < .05\), we reject the null hypothesis. The difference is statistically significant: larger than sampling variation usually produces.
If \(p \geq .05\), we retain the null hypothesis. The data are consistent with no difference in the population.

For a two-sided test at \(\alpha = .05\) with \(df = 199\), the p-value falls below .05 whenever \(t\) is beyond \(\pm 1.97\). This boundary is called the critical value. It gives a quick check when you have a t statistic and no software. With large samples the critical value stays close to \(\pm 1.97\). With 30 cases it is \(\pm 2.05\).
Retaining the null hypothesis leaves the question open. With a larger sample, a small real difference could still emerge. So we write “no statistically significant difference” and avoid “no difference”.

Worked example 4.2

Two budgets, two decisions

The marketing team asks us to test the 200 customers’ spending against two figures: the plan’s 450 USD, and a revised figure of 480 USD. JASP reports:



Table 4.3: Two one-sample t-tests on spending, as reported by JASP





Benchmark, \(\mu_0\)
\(t\)
\(df\)
\(p\)




450 USD
3.064
199
.002


480 USD
1.412
199
.159






For each benchmark, decide whether to reject or retain the null hypothesis at \(\alpha = .05\), and write one sentence on what the decision means for the marketing team.


450 USD: \(p = .002\), which is below .05, so we reject the null hypothesis. The t statistic, 3.06, is also beyond the critical value of 1.97. Our customers spend more than the plan assumed, and the gap is larger than sampling variation usually produces.
480 USD: \(p = .159\), which is above .05, so we retain the null hypothesis. The t statistic, \((505.65 - 480) \div 18.16 = 1.41\), lies inside \(\pm 1.97\). Our mean is 25.65 USD above 480 USD, and a gap of that size arises often between a sample and its population. The revised figure is consistent with our records.




Two errors a test can make
We make each test decision from a sample, so each decision carries a risk of error. Two kinds of error are possible:



Table 4.4: The four outcomes of a test











\(H_0\) true in the population
\(H_0\) untrue in the population




We reject \(H_0\)
Type I error: we report a difference that is absent
Correct decision


We retain \(H_0\)
Correct decision
Type II error: we miss a difference that exists






The significance level sets the probability of a Type I error. At \(\alpha = .05\), if the null hypothesis is true, we reject it in 5 samples out of every 100. The probability of a Type II error depends mostly on the sample size: with a small sample we can miss a real difference, because the standard error is large.
For example: in worked example 4.2 we rejected the null hypothesis for 450 USD. If the population mean is in fact 450 USD, our decision is a Type I error. We retained the null hypothesis for 480 USD. If the population mean is in fact some other figure, such as 500 USD, our decision is a Type II error.






TipTry It 4.2: Name the error



For each case, name the error that would occur, if any.

A bank tests whether its mean waiting time differs from a 10-minute standard. In the population, the mean is 14 minutes. The test gives \(p = .310\).
A retailer tests whether its mean delivery time differs from 3 days. In the population, the mean is exactly 3 days. The test gives \(p = .041\).
A hotel tests whether its guests’ mean spending differs from 200 USD. In the population, the mean is 240 USD. The test gives \(p = .003\).

No error: \(p = .003\) is below .05, so the hotel rejects the null hypothesis, and the population mean does differ from 200 USD.

\(t = 0.54\) lies inside \(\pm 1.97\), so we retain the null hypothesis.
\(p = .590\) is above .05, so we retain the null hypothesis: the same decision.
The mean wait of 45.5 minutes is consistent with the 45-minute promise. The half-minute gap is well within what sampling variation produces.

19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
Effect size and reporting
A p-value tells us whether a gap is larger than sampling variation usually produces. To judge how large the gap is, we compare it with how much the values vary from customer to customer.
For example: our customers spent 55.65 USD more than the plan, and spending varies with a standard deviation of 256.84 USD. The gap is \(55.65 \div 256.84 = 0.22\) of a standard deviation. This measure is Cohen’s d for one sample:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s}\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean, \(\mu_0\) is the benchmark and \(s\) is the standard deviation. Cohen (1988) read 0.2 as small, 0.5 as medium and 0.8 as large, so \(d = 0.22\) is a small effect. JASP prints it as 0.217 beside the p-value.
In APA style: A one-sample t-test showed that mean spending (\(M = 505.65\), \(SD = 256.84\)) was higher than the planned 450 USD, \(t(199) = 3.06\), \(p = .002\), \(d = 0.22\).
For the manager: Customers spend about 56 USD more than the plan assumed, so the revenue forecast is cautious. The effect is small, so the plan needs adjusting more than rethinking.






TipTry It 4.4: Satisfaction against a target



The company aims for a mean satisfaction of 4.0. Across the 200 customers, Satisfaction has a mean of 3.814 and a standard deviation of 0.740.

Calculate the standard error, the t statistic and Cohen’s d.
JASP reports \(p < .001\). Write the result in one APA-style sentence.









NoteCheck your answer






\(SE = 0.740 \div 14.142 = 0.0523\), \(t = (3.814 - 4.0) \div 0.0523 = -3.56\), and \(d = -0.186 \div 0.740 = -0.25\).
Mean satisfaction (\(M = 3.81\), \(SD = 0.74\)) was lower than the target of 4.0, \(t(199) = -3.56\), \(p < .001\), \(d = -0.25\), a small effect.

19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Some outcomes are ordered ratings. Return_Intention records each customer’s intention to return on a 1 to 5 scale. The step from 3 to 4 need not equal the step from 4 to 5, so a mean of these ratings can mislead. For ratings we compare ranks, and test the median.
For example: the manager asks whether customers lean towards returning, which means a typical rating above the scale midpoint of 3. In the file, 115 customers rated above 3, 29 rated below 3 and 56 rated exactly 3. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test sets aside the ratings equal to 3, ranks the remaining distances from 3 by size, and compares the ranks above 3 with the ranks below it.

Worked example 4.3

Intention to return

Test whether the median of Return_Intention differs from 3. Run the test in JASP, read the output, and write the result for the manager.


In JASP: use the same One Sample T-Test panel. Move Return_Intention into Variables, untick Student, tick Wilcoxon signed-rank, set the Test value to 3, and tick Effect size and Descriptives.






Figure 4.3: Wilcoxon signed-rank test of Return_Intention against the scale midpoint of 3



The output: \(V = 8775\) is the sum of the ranks above 3. \(p < .001\), so we reject the null hypothesis. The effect size is the rank-biserial correlation, \(r = .68\). It runs from \(-1\) to \(1\), and about .10 is small, .30 medium and .50 large, so this effect is large. The median rating is 4.
In APA style: Return intention (\(Mdn = 4\)) was higher than the scale midpoint of 3, \(V = 8775\), \(p < .001\), rank-biserial \(r = .68\).
For the manager: most customers lean towards coming back.

19  One mean against a benchmark

title: One mean against a benchmark
text:
Section summary
A sample mean varies from one sample to the next, and the standard error of the mean, \(s / \sqrt{n}\), measures that sampling variation. A test begins from a null hypothesis of no difference and a two-sided alternative. The t statistic divides the gap between a sample mean and a benchmark by the standard error, with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom. Its p-value is the probability of a result at least that far from the benchmark if the null hypothesis is true. At \(\alpha = .05\) we reject the null hypothesis when \(p < .05\), or equally when \(t\) is beyond the critical value of about \(\pm 1.97\). Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error, and retaining an untrue one is a Type II error. In the teaching dataset, customers spent 505.65 USD on average, 55.65 USD above the marketing plan’s 450 USD, \(t(199) = 3.06\), \(p = .002\), \(d = 0.22\). For an ordinal rating, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test compares the median with the benchmark using ranks: return intention (\(Mdn = 4\)) was above the midpoint of 3, \(V = 8775\), \(p < .001\).

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
Learning objectives
After studying this chapter you should be able to:

Choose between the independent samples t-test, the Mann-Whitney U test and the paired t-test from the design and the type of outcome.
Calculate an independent samples t statistic from each group’s mean, standard deviation and size.
Read Levene’s test and choose between Student’s and Welch’s t-test.
Calculate and interpret Cohen’s d, and separate statistical significance from practical significance.
Run the Mann-Whitney U test and the paired t-test in JASP and read their output.
Report each test in APA style and in plain language for a manager.







NoteHow to use this chapter



This week’s learning plan is 9 hours: 1 hour of synchronous lecture, 2 hours of synchronous tutorial and 6 hours of asynchronous self-study. Put your self-study time into the worked examples, the Try It exercises and the checkpoint quiz first.
This chapter builds on chapter 4, which sets out the standard error, the hypotheses, the p-value, the significance level and the two errors. Read that chapter first.
You are permitted to use Google NotebookLM to brainstorm the concepts. Complete the worked examples and the Try It exercises yourself, with no AI assistance. The full policy, and the reason NotebookLM is the only tool permitted, is on the Using AI on This Module page.
This chapter works in JASP. Keep a calculator beside you. One-way ANOVA, for three or more groups, is self-study material and follows in a later update of this chapter.


In chapter 4 we compared one mean with a fixed benchmark. In this chapter we compare two sets of scores, and the first step is to ask how they were collected.

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
section: Which test? Start with the design
text:
Which test? Start with the design
For example: female and male customers are different people, so a comparison of their satisfaction involves two independent groups. A customer’s satisfaction before the event and the same customer’s satisfaction after it are the same person measured twice, so those scores form matched pairs.
The design and the type of outcome together decide the test:



Table 5.1: Choosing a test for two sets of scores










Design
Scale outcome
Ordinal outcome, such as a 1 to 5 rating




Two independent groups
Independent samples t-test
Mann-Whitney U test


The same cases measured twice
Paired samples t-test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test, paired






The t-tests compare means. The Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests compare ranks, so they suit ordinal ratings and scale variables that are clearly skewed in a small sample.
crumbs: Chapter 5: Comparing Groups
20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
The independent samples t-test
Our first question compares the satisfaction of two groups. The file records Gender and Satisfaction, a score from 1 to 5:



Table 5.2: Satisfaction by gender in the teaching dataset











Gender
Customers, \(n\)
Mean satisfaction, \(\bar{x}\)
Standard deviation, \(s\)




Female
112
3.870
0.753


Male
88
3.743
0.722






Female customers rate the event \(3.870 - 3.743 = 0.127\) points higher on average. In chapter 4 we saw that samples of the same customers differ by chance (sampling variation). The question is whether a gap of 0.127 points is larger than that kind of variation.
As in chapter 4, we write the question as two hypotheses about the population:
\[H_0: \mu_{\text{female}} = \mu_{\text{male}} \qquad H_1: \mu_{\text{female}} \neq \mu_{\text{male}}\]
where \(\mu_{\text{female}}\) and \(\mu_{\text{male}}\) are the mean satisfaction of all female and all male customers.

The t statistic for two groups
In chapter 4 we divided the gap between a mean and a benchmark by its standard error (the t statistic). For two groups we divide the gap between the two means by the standard error of that gap:
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{SE_{\text{diff}}}, \qquad SE_{\text{diff}} = s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}\]
where \(\bar{x}_1\) and \(\bar{x}_2\) are the two sample means, \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the two group sizes, and \(s_p\) is the pooled standard deviation, which combines the two groups’ standard deviations into one:
\[s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}}\]
where \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) are the two standard deviations. The denominator, \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\), gives the degrees of freedom: for our groups, \(df = 112 + 88 - 2 = 198\).

Worked example 5.1

Satisfaction and gender

Use Table 5.2: 112 female customers with a mean satisfaction of 3.870 and a standard deviation of 0.753, and 88 male customers with a mean of 3.743 and a standard deviation of 0.722.
Calculate the pooled standard deviation, the standard error of the difference and the t statistic, taking the female group as group 1. Then decide at \(\alpha = .05\).


Step 1, the pooled standard deviation:
\[s_p = \sqrt{\frac{111 \times 0.753^2 + 87 \times 0.722^2}{198}} = \sqrt{\frac{62.94 + 45.35}{198}} = \sqrt{0.547} = 0.740\]
Step 2, the standard error of the difference:
\[SE_{\text{diff}} = 0.740 \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{112} + \frac{1}{88}} = 0.740 \times 0.1425 = 0.1054\]
Step 3, the t statistic:
\[t = \frac{3.870 - 3.743}{0.1054} = \frac{0.127}{0.1054} = 1.21\]
Step 4, the decision: with \(df = 198\) the critical value is \(\pm 1.97\), and 1.21 lies inside it. JASP reports \(t(198) = 1.207\), \(p = .229\). Since \(p\) is above .05, we retain the null hypothesis: the data give no evidence of a difference in satisfaction between female and male customers.









TipTry It 5.1: Waiting time and gender



The 112 female customers waited a mean of 45.277 minutes, with a standard deviation of 12.461. The 88 male customers waited a mean of 45.682 minutes, with a standard deviation of 11.226.

Calculate the pooled standard deviation, to two decimal places.
Calculate the standard error of the difference and the t statistic, taking the female group as group 1.
Decide at \(\alpha = .05\), using the critical value of \(\pm 1.97\).









NoteCheck your answer






\(s_p = \sqrt{(111 \times 12.461^2 + 87 \times 11.226^2) \div 198} = \sqrt{(17{,}234.42 + 10{,}963.09) \div 198} = \sqrt{142.41} = 11.93\) minutes.
\(SE_{\text{diff}} = 11.93 \times 0.1425 = 1.70\), and \(t = (45.277 - 45.682) \div 1.70 = -0.405 \div 1.70 = -0.24\).
\(-0.24\) lies well inside \(\pm 1.97\), so we retain the null hypothesis. Female and male customers wait about the same length of time. JASP gives \(t(198) = -0.238\), \(p = .812\).






Running the test in JASP
Open DMM_Teaching_Data_Full.csv and follow these steps:

Choose T-Tests → Classical → Independent Samples T-Test.
Move Satisfaction into Dependent Variables and Gender into Grouping Variable.







Figure 5.1: The Independent Samples T-Test panel with Satisfaction and Gender assigned




Under Tests, tick Student and Welch.
Under Additional Statistics, tick Effect size, with Cohen’s d, and Descriptives.
Under Assumption Checks, tick Equality of variances and select Levene’s.







Figure 5.2: The test options: Student, Welch, Descriptives, Effect size and Equality of variances



JASP prints three tables: the t-test with a Student row and a Welch row, Levene’s test, and the group descriptives.






Figure 5.3: Independent samples t-test output for Satisfaction by Gender, with Levene’s test









TipIf JASP shows p as 2.175×10⁻²



With Display exact p-values ticked, JASP prints p-values in scientific notation. To show three decimals, open the menu (☰), choose Preferences → Results and untick Display exact p-values. Keep Fix the number of decimals at 3.
crumbs: Chapter 5: Comparing Groups
20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
Levene’s test and Welch’s t-test
The independent samples t-test gives a dependable p-value when three conditions hold:

Independence: each case belongs to one group only. This comes from the study design.
Normality, or large groups: the outcome is roughly normal in each group, or each group holds about 30 cases or more.
Equal variances: the two groups have similar spread.

Levene’s test checks the third condition. Its null hypothesis is that the two population variances are equal, and its p-value decides which row of the output to report:



Table 5.3: Choosing the row from Levene’s test










Levene’s p
Variances
Report




Above .05
Treated as equal
Student’s t-test, the equal-variances row


.05 or below
Unequal
Welch’s t-test, the unequal-variances row






For satisfaction by gender, Levene’s test gives \(F(1, 198) = 0.36\), \(p = .551\), so we report Student’s t-test, as in worked example 5.1.
Welch’s t-test keeps each group’s variance separate. Its standard error is \(\sqrt{s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2}\), and its degrees of freedom come from a longer formula that JASP calculates for us. They are usually a decimal number, which is a quick check that we are reading the Welch row.

Worked example 5.2

Delivery times at two branches (hypothetical)

This example uses hypothetical summary figures, since no comparison in the teaching file has unequal variances. Branch A made 40 deliveries with a mean of 32.5 minutes and a standard deviation of 4.1. Branch B made 25 deliveries with a mean of 35.8 minutes and a standard deviation of 9.6. Levene’s test gives \(p = .003\).
Choose the row to report, calculate the Welch t statistic, and decide at \(\alpha = .05\). Welch’s degrees of freedom are 29.55.


Choice of row: Levene’s \(p = .003\) is .05 or below, so we report Welch’s t-test.
The Welch standard error:
\[SE_{\text{Welch}} = \sqrt{\frac{4.1^2}{40} + \frac{9.6^2}{25}} = \sqrt{0.420 + 3.686} = \sqrt{4.107} = 2.027\]
The t statistic: \(t = (32.5 - 35.8) \div 2.027 = -1.63\).
Decision: with 29.55 degrees of freedom, \(p = .114\), above .05, so we retain the null hypothesis. Reading the Student row by mistake would give \(t(63) = -1.92\), \(p = .060\): the rows differ. Levene’s test therefore comes first.
crumbs: Chapter 5: Comparing Groups
20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
Effect size: Cohen’s d
A p-value tells us whether a gap is larger than sampling variation usually produces. To learn how large the gap is, we need an effect size.
For example: female customers rate the event 0.127 points higher. The pooled standard deviation is 0.740 points (worked example 5.1), so the gap is \(0.127 \div 0.740 = 0.17\) of a standard deviation.
This measure is Cohen’s d: the difference between two means, measured in pooled standard deviations:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p}\]
where the symbols are as in worked example 5.1. Cohen (1988) suggested these benchmarks:



Table 5.4: Benchmarks for Cohen’s d





Size of \(d\), ignoring the sign
Description




0.2
Small


0.5
Medium


0.8
Large






Our satisfaction effect, \(d = 0.17\), is smaller than small. Statistical significance means a difference is larger than sampling variation usually produces. Practical significance means a difference is large enough to change a decision. A report gives both the p-value and Cohen’s d.

20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
Reporting an independent samples t-test
In chapter 2 we reported each result twice, once in APA style and once for a manager (two ways to report a result). A t-test is reported the same way.
In APA style: An independent samples t-test was conducted to compare satisfaction between female and male customers. Levene’s test indicated equal variances, \(F(1, 198) = 0.36\), \(p = .551\). Female customers (\(M = 3.87\), \(SD = 0.75\)) did not differ significantly from male customers (\(M = 3.74\), \(SD = 0.72\)), \(t(198) = 1.21\), \(p = .229\), \(d = 0.17\).
For the manager: Female and male customers are equally satisfied, so one service approach serves both.
Three APA rules apply to every t-test:

The degrees of freedom go in brackets after \(t\): \(t(198)\). Welch’s go to two decimals, \(t(29.55)\).
The p-value has no zero before the point: \(p = .229\), or \(p < .001\).
Cohen’s d keeps its zero: \(d = 0.17\), because d can exceed 1.







TipTry It 5.2: Report the waiting-time result



Use your answer to Try It 5.1. JASP gives \(p = .812\), \(d = -0.03\), and Levene’s \(p = .347\). Write the result in one APA-style sentence and one sentence for the manager.








NoteCheck your answer





Levene’s \(p = .347\) is above .05, so the Student row applies. Female customers (\(M = 45.28\), \(SD = 12.46\)) and male customers (\(M = 45.68\), \(SD = 11.23\)) did not differ significantly in waiting time, \(t(198) = -0.24\), \(p = .812\), \(d = -0.03\). For the manager: both groups wait about 45 minutes, so queue changes affect them alike.

20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
The Mann-Whitney U test
Some outcomes are ordered ratings. Return_Intention records each customer’s intention to return on a 1 to 5 scale, and the gap between a 3 and a 4 need not equal the gap between a 4 and a 5. For such outcomes we compare ranks: all 200 ratings are put in order, and we ask whether one group tends to sit higher in that order than the other. This is the Mann-Whitney U test, the rank-based test for two independent groups.
To run it in JASP, use the same Independent Samples T-Test panel: move Return_Intention into Dependent Variables and Gender into Grouping Variable, untick Student, tick Mann-Whitney, and tick Effect size and Descriptives.






Figure 5.4: Mann-Whitney U test of Return_Intention by Gender



JASP reports \(U = 5164\) and \(p = .547\), so we retain the null hypothesis. Its effect size is the rank-biserial correlation, \(r = -.05\), which runs from \(-1\) to \(1\). About .10 is small, .30 medium and .50 large, so this effect is close to zero. Both groups have a median rating of 4.
In APA style: A Mann-Whitney U test found no significant difference in return intention between female customers (\(Mdn = 4\)) and male customers (\(Mdn = 4\)), \(U = 5164\), \(p = .547\), rank-biserial \(r = -.05\).






TipTry It 5.3: Content ratings and gender



Run a Mann-Whitney U test of Content_Q1, a 1 to 5 rating, by Gender. Report U, p and the two medians, and state your decision.








NoteCheck your answer





\(U = 5563\), \(p = .100\), and both medians are 4. Since \(p\) is above .05, we retain the null hypothesis: the data give no evidence that female and male customers rate the content differently.

20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
The paired samples t-test
Each customer rated satisfaction twice: before the event, in Satisfaction_Pre, and after it, in Satisfaction_Post. The two columns belong to the same people, so we work with each customer’s change: their score after the event minus their score before it.
For example: across the 200 customers, the mean change is \(+0.366\) points, with a standard deviation of 0.376. The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test of these changes against 0, so everything from chapter 4 applies:
\[t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}\]
where \(\bar{d}\) is the mean change, \(s_d\) is the standard deviation of the changes and \(n\) is the number of pairs. Each customer’s own starting level drops out of the changes, so a paired design detects smaller effects than two separate groups.

Worked example 5.3

Satisfaction before and after the event

The mean change in satisfaction is 0.366 points, the standard deviation of the changes is 0.376 and there are 200 pairs. Calculate the t statistic and the degrees of freedom, and decide at \(\alpha = .05\).


The standard error: \(s_d / \sqrt{n} = 0.376 \div 14.142 = 0.0266\).
The t statistic: \(t = 0.366 \div 0.0266 = 13.76\), with \(df = 200 - 1 = 199\).
Decision: 13.76 lies far beyond the critical value of 1.97, and JASP reports \(p < .001\), so we reject the null hypothesis. Satisfaction rose from before the event to after it. The effect size, the mean change divided by its standard deviation, is \(0.366 \div 0.376 = 0.97\), a large effect.



In JASP, choose T-Tests → Classical → Paired Samples T-Test, select Satisfaction_Pre and Satisfaction_Post together and move them into Variable Pairs, then tick Effect size and Descriptives.






Figure 5.5: Paired samples t-test of Satisfaction_Pre against Satisfaction_Post



JASP subtracts the second measure from the first, so it reports \(t = -13.76\) and \(d = -0.97\). The minus sign only shows that the scores after the event are higher. In a report we state the direction in words.
In APA style: A paired samples t-test showed that satisfaction rose from before the event (\(M = 3.77\), \(SD = 0.77\)) to after it (\(M = 4.14\), \(SD = 0.76\)), \(t(199) = -13.76\), \(p < .001\), \(d = -0.97\).






TipTry It 5.4: Content and value ratings



The same customers rated content (Content_Q1) and value (Value_Q1), both on a 1 to 5 scale.

Which test fits, given that both ratings are ordinal?
Run it in JASP: use the Paired Samples T-Test panel with Wilcoxon signed-rank ticked in place of Student. Report V and p.









NoteCheck your answer






The paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test: the same customers gave both ratings, and both are ordinal.
\(V = 7241\), \(p = .004\). Content is rated higher than value, with means of 3.96 and 3.67 and a median of 4 for both.
crumbs: Chapter 5: Comparing Groups
20  Comparing two groups and paired data

title: Comparing two groups and paired data
text:
Section summary
The design decides the test. Two independent groups with a scale outcome call for the independent samples t-test, and with an ordinal outcome for the Mann-Whitney U test. The same cases measured twice call for the paired samples t-test. Levene’s test chooses the row of the independent t-test: above .05 we report Student’s t-test, and at .05 or below Welch’s, which has decimal degrees of freedom. Cohen’s d measures the gap in standard deviations, with 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 as small, medium and large. In the teaching dataset, female and male customers did not differ significantly in satisfaction, \(t(198) = 1.21\), \(p = .229\), \(d = 0.17\), and satisfaction rose from before the event to after it, \(t(199) = -13.76\), \(p < .001\).
